title: Chapter 69: Fire at the Edge, Part 4 of 5: Robin First
html:
She screamed his name. He did not stop.
He went into the burning tent the way the Erasers had gone into the thorns. Straight through. He pulled the flap aside with his bare gray hand, and the flap was on fire, and he did not let go of it. He ducked under, limping, on his stiff leg, without his crutch, and the smoke came pouring out round him, and he was gone.
Lyra stood there with her sword in her hand.
The tent burned. The whole roof of it was alight now, the hide curling and blackening, the bent-thorn frame showing through in black ribs. The smoke came out of the smoke hole in a thick black column and the wind took it and laid it over the camp. She could hear the fire inside. A roaring. A crackling. And the screaming. Thin and high and young.
And then the screaming changed. Got louder. Closer.
And Corin came out.
He came out backward, bent double, dragging. In each of his gray hands he had a fistful of cloth. The collar of a tunic. Two collars. And on the end of each collar, a child. Two of them. Small. Kicking and screaming and coughing, their faces black with smoke, their round shaved heads shining with sweat. He dragged them out of the door of the burning tent by their collars, the way you drag a sack, backward, onto the gravel, and fell over on top of them, and rolled off, and lay on his back on the frozen ground with his chest heaving.
His hands were smoking.
Lyra saw it. Thin gray threads of smoke going up from the backs of his gray hands and his fingers and the cuffs of his coat. The cuffs were burning. Small yellow flames, licking at the cloth. He did not seem to notice. He was lying on his back looking up at the black sky, coughing.
She dropped to her knees beside him and beat at the flames on his cuffs with her gloved hands until they went out. The cloth was charred. The skin of his wrists under it was red. But his hands. His gray hands. They were not red. They were not blistered. They were only gray, the same dull smooth stone-gray as always, with the black fingertips, and smoking a little, like a stone taken out of a fire.
They had not burned.
She did not know if that was good.
The two children had rolled away from him and were sitting up, coughing, crying, alive. A woman came running out of the smoke and fell on her knees beside them and gathered them both up in her arms and ran.
Corin sat up. His face was black with soot. His eyes were streaming.
"There are more," he said. Hoarse. "In the next one. I heard them."
And he got up. Without his crutch. On his stiff leg. And started toward the next burning tent.
Lyra looked round.
The camp was burning. The whole south half of it. A wall of fire, tent after tent, going up in the wind, with the smoke rolling over everything. People were running in every direction. Goats were everywhere. The Ashborn men had stopped trying to stop the Erasers with their broken spears and were running into the burning tents too, now, like Corin, and coming out with people. Old ones. Babies. Children. But not fast enough. There were too many tents and too much fire and too few of them, and they were running everywhere at once, and nobody was telling anybody anything.
And the children were still in there. She could hear them. In the tents. Crying. In the smoke.
And from somewhere, from a long way off, a voice came back to her. A man's voice. Wat's. Hoarse and broken, in a turf hut in the fens, with the boy asleep against his side, telling them how it had been at the end, on the burning barge, with the red sail on fire over Hessa's head. She didn't stop to think, Wat had said. She didn't look at the fire. She just held the boy out to me over the side, and she said it, like an order.
Go. Robin first.
Lyra stood up.
She did not think. She did not decide. She stood up in the middle of the burning camp with her sword in her hand, and she filled her lungs with smoke, and she shouted. Louder than she had ever shouted in her life. Louder than she had shouted Corin's name in the ring.
"Robin first!"
The Ashborn nearest her turned and stared at her.
They did not know who Robin was. They could not have. They had never heard the name. But they heard her. They heard the voice. And Lyra saw them understand. Not the words. The sound. The sound of somebody who knew what to do, telling them.
"Robin first!" she shouted again. And pointed. At the tents. At the crying. "The children! The children first! Get the children out first! Then the rest!"
And Kestrel, somewhere in the smoke, took it up.
Lyra heard her. One word, in the round Ashborn speech, very loud and very clear, like a bell. And then another word. And the Ashborn who had been running everywhere at once stopped running everywhere at once, and turned, all of them, toward the tents. Toward the crying.
Children first.
They went in. Men and women. Into the smoke. Into the burning tents, one after another, along the row. And came out with children. Dragging them, carrying them, throwing them out through the flaps onto the gravel to the ones waiting outside, who caught them and ran with them north, away from the fire, toward the ridge.
Corin came out of the second tent with a baby under one arm, wrapped in a smoldering fur. He gave it to a woman without looking at her and went back in.
Oren came past Lyra at a run with a small boy over his shoulder like a sack of meal, and a little girl under the other arm, and his notched sword in his teeth.
Arran came out of the smoke with two girls by the hand, and his flute bouncing on its cord round his neck, and his face streaked black and white with soot and tears, and he was shouting too. The same thing. Robin first. In the round Ashborn speech, so that it came out strange. Robin first. Robin first. As if it were a word the Ashborn had always had.
And through it all, through the fire and the children and the smoke, the four iron shapes walked north. Ticking.
The first one had reached Corin's tent.
Lyra saw it. The last tent at the north edge of the camp, before the ridge, with the six or seven old faded handprints on it and Old Hask's small new one. The Eraser walked up to it. Its long iron arm came up. And it tore the side of the tent open, the way you tear a sheet of paper. The hide ripped. The frame of bent thorn snapped. The Eraser bent its blank iron head and looked in through the slit in its face.
At the empty furs inside.
And straightened up.
And turned its head. Slowly. Smooth. With a whirr of brass.
Looking for him.
And Lyra, standing in the middle of the burning camp, saw its blank head turn, and turn, and stop.
On the other three.
They had not come to the tent. They had stopped, all three, in the middle of the camp. By the bread racks. Their heads turned.
To the bread racks.
Where three small children were standing with their backs against the wooden poles, between the racks of flat dark loaves, in the smoke, holding hands. Too frightened to run. Staring up at the nearest iron shape.
It had not come for them. Lyra knew that. It did not want them. It was only walking. North. Toward Corin. And they were in the way.
And it was not going to stop.
Lyra Burns
She was eight paces away.
She knew it the way she knew everything, without thinking, by counting. Eight paces. From where she stood in the smoke, with her sword in her hand, to the bread rack. To the three children with their backs against the poles. To the iron shape walking toward them.
It was the fourth one. The one from the east end of the line. It had gone round the far side of the big fire, through the smoke, and now it was coming up between the bread racks, north, toward the ridge, toward the torn tent where Corin was not. Its blank head was turned north. It was not looking at the children at all.
And they were in its way.
Three of them. Small. The biggest no higher than Lyra's waist. She knew them. She saw it now, through the smoke, in the red light of the fires. The girl who had thrown her spear down at noon. The little boy with the runny nose, who had pulled her into the dance. And another, a tiny one, a girl, with her thumb in her mouth. Holding hands. Backed up against the bread rack, with the racks of flat dark loaves on either side of them and the wooden poles behind, and nowhere to go. Staring up at it.
It walked on.
It did not slow. It was going to walk through them the way it had walked through the thorns. Not because it wanted to. Because they were there. Because it did not stop. And its iron foot would come down, and its iron arm would come up and move them aside, the way it had moved the old woman, the way it had moved Brin. And they were so small.
Seven paces.
Lyra was moving. She did not remember starting to move. She was running, in her clumsy felt-wrapped feet, across the gravel, through the smoke, with her sword up.
And she knew she could not do it.
Not like this. Not with what was in her arms. She had parried two hundred and one cuts that afternoon with what was in her arms, and her arms were lead, and they shook, and the thing in front of her was made of iron. Oren had cut it three times with all his strength and left a scratch and a notch. She had seen. There was nothing in her arms that could stop that. Nothing at all.
Six paces.
And her hand went inside. For the fire.
She felt it go. The old way. The way Oren had spent all afternoon beating out of her. Her hand went inside herself, quick, reaching, for something, anything, something to burn.
And this time she did not stop it.
Because there was a fire here. They were not on the Glass. Not yet. Not for one more night. There was a fire here, all round her, and inside her, and it was still hers, and three children were standing against a bread rack, and she was five paces away.
She reached.
And the thing that came to her hand was the dance.
She did not choose it. She had never chosen. You did not choose, when you burned. You reached in, and the first thing your hand closed on was the thing that went. The nearest. The warmest. The one at the top.
And the nearest, the warmest, the one right at the top, was an hour old.
One, two, three. And lift. And turn.
The hall at Crown Walk. The black and white floor. The gold light through the tall windows. Her mother bending down, holding both her hands. Counting. One, two, three. And turn. Her mother's skirts brushing her face. Her mother's voice, laughing.
And tonight. The drums. The flute going in and out like a swallow. The children's hands in hers. Her feet finding it, all on their own, after all those years. Her head back. Laughing.
That's what it sounds like.
She held it in her hand for one breath.
Four paces.
She thought: no. Not this. Not this one. Anything but this one. I only just got it back.
Three paces.
The little boy with the runny nose was looking at her. Past the iron. Straight at her, with his round frightened face. The way he had looked up at her when he pulled her into the ring.
She let it go.
It went into the fire like a feather. Like nothing. Light, and quick, and gone. One, two, three, and lift, and turn, and her mother counting, and the gold light, and the drums, and her own laugh with her head back, all of it, gone. Into the fire. Into the flames inside her. And the flames came up.
They came up into her arms like a wind.
She was two paces behind it. She was behind it. It had not turned. It did not know she was there. Its iron back was in front of her, broad, dark, plated, with the brass of the joints shining at the shoulders. And in the small of the back, low down, there was a plate. A square one. Bigger than the others. Brass-edged. With a hole in the middle of it, where a key would go.
She did not aim. The fire aimed for her. It always had.
She struck.
One cut. One. A single stroke, from behind, from below, rising. With everything. With the dance and the drums and her mother's hands and the gold light and her own laugh. All of it, in one stroke, through the steel and into the iron.
The wind-severing cut.
Her father's fencing master had called it that, long ago, in the yard at Crown Walk, when she was twelve. The one stroke that went through anything, if you put enough behind it. You only ever do it once, he had said. In a whole life, perhaps. If you are lucky, never.
She did it.
The blade went in at the bottom edge of the square brass-edged plate in the small of the Eraser's back. And through it. Through the iron. She felt it go through, the way you feel a needle go through thick cloth, a resistance and then nothing. And on. Into what was behind the plate. Into something that was coiled, and tight, and humming, and alive the way a clock is alive.
And cut it.
There was a sound.
Lyra had never heard a sound like it. A sound like a scream. Like a bird screaming, high and thin and rising, rising, rising. Like a thousand threads snapping one after another so fast that they made a single note. Metal. Singing.
The Eraser stopped.
One pace from the bread rack. One pace from the three children. It stopped. Its iron foot was lifted, for the next step, and it stayed lifted, and the iron arm that had been coming up to move them aside stopped halfway, in the air.
The ticking stopped.
Not slowed. Stopped. In the middle of a tick.
And the scream of the metal went on, rising, inside it, higher and higher, until it was so high Lyra could hardly hear it, and the iron plates of the thing's back began to shake. To rattle. To bulge outward, as if something inside were trying to get out.
And then something did.
The Spring
The back plate burst.
It came off the Eraser's iron back all at once, the whole square brass-edged plate, torn open along the line of her cut, and flew out sideways, spinning, and hit the bread rack with a crash and knocked a whole row of hard dark loaves onto the ground.
And out of the hole where it had been, something came.
Lyra saw it. In the firelight. For one long moment it seemed to hang in the air, the way things do when you see them and cannot believe them. A coil. A great flat coil of brass, gleaming gold, as wide across as a cartwheel's hub, wound tight round and round itself like the shell of a snail, like the inside of a clock. The mainspring. Cut through on one side, where her blade had gone in, and unwinding.
It came out of the hole in the Eraser's back unwinding. Opening. Flinging itself open, the cut end lashing round and round, faster and faster, the long bright band of brass uncoiling into the air in great looping whips, singing. That was the scream. That was the high thin rising note. It was the spring, unwinding, all the strength that had been wound into it coming out at once.
Lyra threw herself flat.
The band of brass went over her head. She felt the wind of it. It lashed out across the camp, uncoiling, a long gleaming whip of gold, and cut through the corner of the bread rack like a knife through butter, and sliced the top off a pole, and hit the gravel beside her with a crack like a shot and threw up a spray of stones.
And went on. Out. Away. Still unwinding. Still singing. Out of the firelight, into the dark, over the snow at the edge of the camp, a long loop of gold flashing in the light of the burning tents, turning over and over, and then down. Into the snow. With a hiss.
The singing stopped.
It was very quiet.
Lyra lifted her head.
The Eraser was standing exactly where it had stopped. One pace from the bread rack. One iron foot lifted. One iron arm half raised. Its blank head turned north. There was a ragged square hole in the middle of its back, low down, and through the hole she could see wheels. Brass wheels, little and big, with teeth, all stopped. Rods. Pins. A tangle of fine bright wire. Nothing moving. Nothing at all.
It did not tick.
And then, slowly, the way a tree goes when it has been cut almost through and the last of the wood gives, it leaned.
Forward. Toward the bread rack. Toward the three children.
Lyra was up. On her knees. Too slow. Too far.
But the children had moved. The girl who had thrown her spear had them both by the hands, and she was dragging them. Sideways. Out from between the racks. Out of the way. She had seen it lean, and she had moved, and she had not let go of either of them.
The Eraser fell.
It came down on the bread rack with a crash that shook the ground. The poles snapped. The racks went over. Hundreds of hard dark flat loaves went everywhere, bouncing and rolling across the gravel, the way the turnips had gone out of Garrett's cart. And the great iron body lay among them on its face, with its lifted foot still lifted and its half-raised arm still half raised, and did not move.
The three children stood a little way off and stared at it.
Lyra got up.
She was shaking all over. Her arms. Her legs. Her hands on the hilt of her sword. She looked down at the blade and it was notched, the way Oren's was, a bite out of it near the guard where it had gone through the plate. And there was something on it. A smear of black oil.
She went to the fallen Eraser.
She did not know why. She did not decide to. Her feet took her there. And she stood over it, among the scattered loaves, and looked down at the ragged square hole in its iron back.
There was a piece of the spring still inside. The end of it. The part that had been fixed to the middle of the coil, at the center, where the key would wind it. A short thick stub of brass, curved, bright. Still bolted to a drum. A little brass drum, round and flat, about the size of the palm of her hand, at the heart of the wheels.
And there was a mark on the drum.
It caught the firelight. That was why she saw it. A small bright place on the dull brass, where something had been stamped into the metal, very small and very deep and very neat. The way a maker stamps his mark on his work.
She bent closer.
A square.
A tiny square, no bigger than her smallest fingernail. With lines inside it. Crossing it. Corner to corner, and across. And the corners turned in, very slightly, toward the middle. Like a piece of paper, folded small.
Lyra stared at it.
She knew it. She knew she knew it. From somewhere. From a long time ago. Something in her went cold and quick, the way it did when she heard a step on a stair that she knew but could not place.
From somewhere.
And then, behind her, very close, there was a sound. Not ticking. A scream. A human scream. Kestrel's voice, high and terrible, a single word in the round Ashborn speech, and then the same word in the southern way, so that everyone would understand it.
"Run!"
Lyra turned.
The other three were coming back.
They had stopped, all three, when the fourth one fell. She saw that. They had stopped where they were, among the burning tents, and their blank iron heads had turned. All three. Toward the fallen one. Toward the bread rack. Toward her.
And past her.
To Corin.
He was standing by the torn tent at the north edge of the camp, with a child in his arms, in the smoke. And all three blank heads swung toward him at once, with a whirr of brass, and stopped. And held.
And the ticking started again. Faster. Louder. All three together.
And they came.
She did not have time to think about the little folded square on the brass. Not then. She did not have time to think about anything at all.
